profiles.title: Root-zone oxygen stress
profiles.overview: A saturated root zone can look like thirst because oxygen-starved roots stop moving water efficiently.

signals.reason: Droop, yellowing, or stalled growth fits oxygen stress
The medium stays wet for an extended period
Drainage is restricted
The pattern affects older leaves or the whole plant

checks: Lift the container and compare its weight with a known dry container.
Check whether the top layer is dry while the lower root zone remains wet.
Confirm every drainage opening is clear and the pot never sits in runoff.
actions: Pause watering until the root zone reaches an appropriate dryback for this plant type.
Increase gentle air exchange around the container and empty standing runoff.
If the mix remains saturated for days, move to a clean, airier medium while disturbing healthy roots as little as possible.
profiles.avoid: Do not add fertilizer to a saturated root zone or water again simply because leaves are drooping.

profiles.title: Water deficit
profiles.overview: A dry root ball loses pressure quickly, producing limp leaves, crisp margins, and slowed growth.

signals.reason: Wilt, crisp tissue, or slow growth fits water deficit
The medium becomes very dry
Water passes through quickly
Young roots have little moisture reserve

checks: Probe below the surface; dry peat can repel water while appearing wet on top.
Look for a gap between the root ball and container wall.
Compare morning and evening posture to see whether heat accelerates wilting.
actions: Rehydrate slowly in two or three passes so the full root ball absorbs water.
Let excess water drain, then use container weight and root-zone feel to set the next watering.
Add a light mulch outdoors or reduce excessive airflow around very small containers.
profiles.avoid: Avoid leaving the pot standing in water after rehydration or switching to a rigid calendar schedule.

profiles.title: Root rot or severe root decline
profiles.overview: Soft, dark, foul-smelling roots point to advanced root damage and microbial decay rather than a simple watering miss.

signals.reason: Soft roots or a sour odor is a high-value root-rot signal
The canopy symptoms fit declining roots
Persistent saturation favors root decline
The issue centers on the crown, roots, or whole plant

checks: Inspect several roots, not only one stained section; healthy roots are usually firm for their species.
Smell the medium near the crown and check for a soft stem base.
Review water temperature and aeration in hydro systems.
actions: Separate the plant and sanitize tools before using them elsewhere.
Remove clearly dead root material with clean tools and move viable tissue into fresh, well-aerated medium.
Correct standing water, blocked drainage, excessive reservoir warmth, or weak hydro aeration before replanting.
profiles.avoid: Do not reuse the old medium or return contaminated tools to healthy plants without cleaning them.

profiles.title: Compacted or poorly aerated medium
profiles.overview: Dense medium can stay wet in the center, shed water at the edges, and limit fine-root growth at the same time.

signals.reason: Water movement through the root zone is restricted
The canopy shows reduced root performance
Root condition still needs inspection
Soil structure can compact over time

checks: Time how long irrigation takes to enter and leave the root zone.
Push a clean skewer through several areas and feel for dense layers.
Check whether roots occupy only the outside of a heavy, wet core.
actions: Open blocked drainage and remove standing runoff immediately.
At the next appropriate repot, use a structure suited to the species with durable air space.
For garden soil, improve structure gradually and avoid working it while waterlogged.
profiles.avoid: Avoid repeatedly poking or tearing through a living root ball as a substitute for a proper medium correction.

profiles.title: Root-bound container
profiles.overview: A tightly occupied container can dry too fast, resist even watering, and limit new growth.

signals.reason: Circling or densely packed roots directly support this pattern
The root zone loses water quickly
Growth and hydration symptoms fit a crowded root zone
The plant is in a container medium

checks: Slide the root ball out carefully and check whether roots form a dense wall.
Look for water channeling directly down the pot edge.
Compare canopy size with container volume and species habit.
actions: Move one practical pot size larger using compatible fresh medium.
Gently free only the outer circling roots when the species tolerates it.
Water the newly potted root ball evenly and shelter it from extreme conditions during recovery.
profiles.avoid: Avoid jumping to an oversized container that will remain wet far longer than the active roots can use.

profiles.title: Transplant or relocation shock
profiles.overview: A recent move can briefly reduce water uptake while roots and leaves adjust to a new environment.

signals.reason: Symptoms followed a transplant or move
The response fits an adjustment period
The plant is still establishing
Visible roots appear healthy

checks: Confirm the root ball is moist but aerated.
Compare the old and new light, temperature, wind, and humidity.
Watch whether new growth remains firm even if a few older leaves decline.
actions: Keep conditions steady and protect the plant from harsh midday light or wind for several days.
Water according to the actual root ball, not the larger volume of new medium.
Remove only tissue that is fully dead; keep functioning leaves during recovery.
profiles.avoid: Avoid stacking extra fertilizer, pruning, and another move onto the same recovery period.

profiles.title: Nitrogen shortage
profiles.overview: Nitrogen is mobile in plants, so a true shortage usually begins as an even paling of older leaves.

signals.reason: Paling and slow growth can reflect low nitrogen
Older leaves are affected first
There was no abrupt environmental change
Active growth raises nitrogen demand

checks: Confirm the yellowing is even rather than between green veins.
Check root health and pH before assuming the nutrient is absent.
Review feed concentration, irrigation frequency, and the age of the medium.
actions: Correct root-zone pH and watering first if either is outside the plant's range.
Use a complete, species-appropriate fertilizer at the label's gentle end, then watch new growth.
Judge recovery by healthier new leaves; badly yellowed leaves may not become green again.
profiles.avoid: Avoid a large one-time nitrogen dose, especially during late flowering or on a stressed root system.

profiles.title: Excess nitrogen
profiles.overview: Very dark foliage, glossy leaves, and downward clawing often follow a feed that supplies more nitrogen than the plant can use.

signals.reason: Downward clawing is a classic excess-feed pattern
Feed strength recently increased
Excess nitrogen is especially disruptive in reproductive growth
Water balance appears less likely as the main cause

checks: Compare leaf color and gloss with healthy growth from the same plant type.
Review every source of fertilizer, including amended soil and supplements.
Measure runoff or reservoir strength only as a trend, using a calibrated meter.
actions: Stop adding high-nitrogen products and return to a balanced, label-compliant program.
In hydro or coco, replace or dilute an overly strong solution with correctly balanced feed.
In soil, allow normal irrigation and plant uptake to reduce excess rather than repeatedly flooding the pot.
profiles.avoid: Avoid aggressive flushing in dense soil; it can replace one stress with oxygen loss.

profiles.title: Nutrient burn or salt buildup
profiles.overview: Concentrated fertilizer salts draw water from roots and commonly show first as burned tips and margins.

signals.reason: Burned tips and edges fit salt stress
Symptoms followed stronger feeding
Container culture can accumulate salts
Dryback concentrates dissolved salts

checks: Inspect whether damage begins at leaf tips and progresses inward.
Verify meter calibration, concentrate mixing order, and total product dose.
Check for a white crust on the medium or container.
actions: Reduce feed strength and restore a balanced root-zone solution appropriate to the medium.
Remove accumulated runoff and make sure irrigation wets the root zone evenly.
Resume feeding gradually only after new growth looks stable.
profiles.avoid: Do not chase damaged leaves with additional supplements; burnt tissue will not repair itself.

profiles.title: Root-zone pH imbalance
profiles.overview: Several deficiencies appearing together often mean nutrients are present but chemically less available at the roots.

signals.reason: Measured pH is outside the target range
Mixed nutrient-like symptoms fit availability problems
Multiple areas are affected
Roots look viable despite canopy symptoms

checks: Calibrate the pH meter with fresh standards before trusting a reading.
Measure the solution going in and a representative root-zone sample.
Check alkalinity and fertilizer mixing order if pH drifts repeatedly.
actions: Adjust gradually toward the range appropriate for the plant and medium.
Stabilize irrigation and recheck after the root zone has equilibrated.
Use a complete base nutrient before layering single-element additives.
profiles.avoid: Avoid large back-and-forth pH corrections or combining concentrated adjusters directly with fertilizer.

profiles.title: Magnesium shortage
profiles.overview: Magnesium shortage typically creates interveinal yellowing on older leaves while veins stay greener.

signals.reason: Interveinal paling supports magnesium stress
Magnesium symptoms usually begin on older leaves
Soilless systems need a balanced magnesium supply
pH can reduce magnesium availability

checks: Compare older and newer leaves; the older set should lead the pattern.
Check pH and total feed before adding a magnesium-only product.
Review source water and whether calcium-heavy inputs are unbalancing the solution.
actions: Correct pH and use a complete fertilizer formulated for the medium.
If the base feed truly lacks magnesium, add a labeled magnesium source at the low end of its rate.
Track new growth over several days instead of expecting old mottling to disappear.
profiles.avoid: Avoid repeated magnesium dosing without confirming the pattern; excess can interfere with other nutrients.

profiles.title: Calcium delivery problem
profiles.overview: Calcium problems show on developing tissue as irregular spots, weak edges, or distorted new growth and are often tied to roots or transpiration.

signals.reason: Damage is concentrated in developing tissue
Newest leaves are affected first
Very humid air can slow calcium movement
Soilless media require deliberate calcium balance

checks: Inspect the newest leaves and growing tip closely.
Confirm roots are active and the root zone is neither saturated nor extremely dry.
Review pH, source water, and the complete nutrient label before supplementing.
actions: Stabilize root moisture and gentle air movement around new growth.
Correct pH and use a balanced feed designed for the medium.
Add calcium only when the water and base fertilizer analysis show a real gap.
profiles.avoid: Avoid heavy calcium additions; they can create new potassium or magnesium imbalances.

profiles.title: Potassium shortage
profiles.overview: A potassium shortage commonly progresses from marginal yellowing to scorched edges on older leaves.

signals.reason: Marginal scorch supports potassium stress
Older leaves tend to show first
Demand can rise during flowering and fruiting
pH may be restricting uptake

checks: Confirm damage starts at margins rather than as random lesions.
Check root health and pH before raising potassium.
Review whether a high level of another nutrient could be competing for uptake.
actions: Restore the correct pH and a complete flowering or fruiting feed for the species.
Increase potassium only within the product label and in small steps.
Keep irrigation even so concentration swings do not worsen margin burn.
profiles.avoid: Avoid high-dose bloom boosters; an excess can resemble or create other deficiencies.

profiles.title: Phosphorus stress
profiles.overview: Slow growth, dull foliage, and red-purple coloration can reflect phosphorus stress, but temperature and genetics must be ruled out.

signals.reason: Color and slowed growth can fit phosphorus stress
Cold roots can sharply reduce phosphorus uptake
The pattern is widespread or begins low
Reproductive growth raises phosphorus demand

checks: Compare the color with the plant's normal genetics and healthy stems.
Measure root-zone temperature, not only room temperature.
Confirm pH and overall feed balance.
actions: Warm the root zone gradually into the species-appropriate range.
Correct pH and use a complete feed rather than a single heavy phosphorus dose.
Monitor new growth and flowering performance for improvement.
profiles.avoid: Avoid treating every purple stem as a deficiency; light, cold, and genetics can produce the same color.

profiles.title: Iron or manganese availability problem
profiles.overview: Pale tissue between greener veins on the newest leaves often points to an immobile micronutrient availability issue.

signals.reason: Newest tissue shows interveinal or pale growth
The growing tip is affected first
High pH commonly reduces iron and manganese availability
Roots appear capable of recovery

checks: Confirm older leaves are greener than the newest set.
Verify pH with a calibrated meter and review water alkalinity.
Check whether roots are cold, damaged, or saturated.
actions: Bring root-zone pH gradually into the medium's target range.
Use a complete micronutrient package suited to the medium if the base feed lacks one.
Evaluate the color of new leaves; old bleached tissue may remain pale.
profiles.avoid: Avoid spraying concentrated iron solutions or adding multiple micronutrient products at once.

profiles.title: Sulfur or zinc shortage
profiles.overview: Uniform pale new growth or small, distorted leaves can come from less common sulfur or zinc problems, often secondary to pH.

signals.reason: Pale, small, or distorted new growth fits a micronutrient issue
The newest tissue is most affected
High pH can limit zinc availability
There is no obvious acute event

checks: Rule out iron-related interveinal chlorosis and calcium-related spots first.
Review the complete fertilizer label for sulfur and trace elements.
Confirm pH and inspect the root system.
actions: Correct the root environment before adding an isolated element.
Use a complete trace-element product only if the base program has a documented gap.
Photograph the newest node and compare its development after one week.
profiles.avoid: Avoid guessing between trace elements from color alone; symptoms overlap heavily.

profiles.title: Excess light or lamp stress
profiles.overview: Intense light can bleach upper leaves, curl margins upward, and create dry patches closest to the source.

signals.reason: Bleaching and upward curl fit excess light
Damage is strongest near the light
Light intensity is high
Symptoms followed a light change

checks: Compare exposed leaves with shaded leaves on the same plant.
Check leaf-surface temperature at the brightest point.
Confirm the lamp distance and dimmer setting against the manufacturer's guidance.
actions: Reduce intensity or increase distance in a small step.
Acclimate the plant over several days before raising light again.
Keep water and airflow steady while healthy new tissue develops.
profiles.avoid: Avoid making a large light reduction and a major feeding change on the same day.

profiles.title: Insufficient light
profiles.overview: Too little usable light leads to weak, stretched growth, slow water use, and gradual yellowing.

signals.reason: The plant receives limited light
Slow, pale growth fits low energy input
Low light slows water use
The decline is broad or begins with older leaves

checks: Observe whether stems lean or stretch toward the light.
Compare actual hours of useful light with the species' needs.
Check whether watering frequency stayed high as seasonal light declined.
actions: Move the plant toward brighter indirect light or add a suitable grow light gradually.
Reduce watering frequency as light and water use decline.
Rotate the container regularly once growth stabilizes.
profiles.avoid: Avoid moving a shade-adapted plant directly into harsh sun without acclimation.

profiles.title: Heat stress
profiles.overview: High leaf temperature increases water demand and commonly causes upward curl, wilt, and crisp edges.

signals.reason: Heat spikes are present
Curling and wilt fit excess heat
The root zone dries rapidly
Conditions changed recently

checks: Measure temperature at leaf height during the hottest part of the cycle.
Check direct sun, radiant heat, and lamp heat separately.
Confirm roots remain moist enough without becoming waterlogged.
actions: Reduce peak heat with shade, greater lamp distance, or improved room ventilation.
Water thoroughly at an appropriate time, then let excess drain.
Increase gentle air mixing without aiming a strong fan directly at damaged leaves.
profiles.avoid: Avoid ice water or abrupt temperature shocks.

profiles.title: Cold root zone or chilling injury
profiles.overview: Cold slows roots and nutrient movement, producing wilt, dark patches, purple color, and stalled growth.

signals.reason: The plant experiences cold conditions
The symptom pattern fits chilling
A location or weather shift occurred
Exposure affects broad or tender tissue

checks: Measure the root-zone low overnight.
Look for damage closest to glass, vents, or outdoor exposure.
Distinguish firm dark pigmentation from soft frost-damaged tissue.
actions: Move the plant away from drafts and warm it gradually.
Let cold, wet medium dry toward the plant's normal range before watering again.
Wait for the extent of tissue damage to declare itself before pruning.
profiles.avoid: Avoid placing chilled tissue next to a heater or applying fertilizer before roots resume activity.

profiles.title: Dry-air stress
profiles.overview: Very dry air can outpace root water delivery and produce crisp margins, curl, and tender-tip damage.

signals.reason: Air is very dry
Margins and posture fit dry-air stress
Tender or broad tissue is involved
This plant group is often sensitive to dry air

checks: Measure humidity near the leaves rather than across the room.
Check for hot vents or strong fans that create a localized dry zone.
Confirm the root ball is hydrating evenly.
actions: Move the plant away from heating vents and direct fan streams.
Group compatible plants or use a controlled humidifier with regular cleaning.
Keep humidity stable; target ranges vary by species and growth stage.
profiles.avoid: Avoid constant leaf misting as the only fix, especially where leaves stay wet overnight.

profiles.title: Edema from water imbalance
profiles.overview: When roots absorb water faster than leaves release it, cells can rupture and leave corky spots or bumps.

signals.reason: Humid air slows transpiration
Roots have a steady surplus of water
Spotting or blister-like damage can fit edema
Cool conditions further slow water use

checks: Look for raised, corky areas, often on the undersides of leaves.
Compare nighttime humidity and root moisture.
Rule out insects and spreading leaf-spot lesions.
actions: Allow a more appropriate dryback and improve gentle air exchange.
Water earlier in the active light period rather than before a cool, humid night.
Keep foliage dry and stabilize temperature.
profiles.avoid: Avoid treating corky edema as an infectious disease unless lesions are actively spreading.

profiles.title: Wind or fan burn
profiles.overview: Continuous strong airflow dehydrates the exposed side of a plant and can twist or crisp leaf edges.

signals.reason: Curling and edge damage fit mechanical drying
Damage is localized to exposed tissue
Dry air magnifies fan stress
Air exposure may have changed with location

checks: Look for damage mainly on the side facing a vent or fan.
Observe whether leaves are constantly whipping rather than gently moving.
Check whether the fan cycle continues during the driest period.
actions: Redirect or diffuse airflow so leaves move gently.
Move the plant outside the direct stream while keeping room air exchanged.
Trim only fully dead edges once the source is corrected.
profiles.avoid: Avoid turning off all circulation in a humid growing area.

profiles.title: Spider mites
profiles.overview: Fine stippling, moving dots under leaves, and delicate webbing form a strong spider-mite pattern.

signals.reason: Webbing or moving dots is a high-value mite signal
Stippling and webbing fit feeding damage
Mites often spread from localized leaf undersides

checks: Use a hand lens on leaf undersides and tap a leaf over white paper.
Inspect nearby plants, stakes, and container rims.
Mark several leaves to see whether stippling expands.
actions: Isolate the plant and remove the most heavily infested leaves in a sealed bag.
Rinse leaf undersides where the plant tolerates it, then use a product labeled for the plant and pest.
Repeat inspection and label-directed treatment because eggs may survive a single pass.
profiles.avoid: Avoid spraying oils or soaps under intense light, on heat-stressed plants, or directly onto flowers meant for consumption.

profiles.title: Thrips
profiles.overview: Silvery scars, black waste specks, and distorted young leaves commonly indicate thrips feeding.

signals.reason: Black specks or silvery scars strongly support thrips
Tender growth shows scraping damage
New growth or scattered leaves are affected

checks: Open folded new leaves and inspect with a hand lens.
Tap flowers or leaves over white paper and watch for slender moving insects.
Use blue or yellow sticky cards to monitor adults, not as the sole treatment.
actions: Isolate the plant and remove badly damaged tissue.
Use a label-approved integrated pest treatment that covers both leaves and the relevant life stage in the medium.
Reinspect new growth frequently and treat on the product's labeled interval.
profiles.avoid: Avoid using unregistered pesticide mixtures or applying products to edible tissue unless the label explicitly permits it.

profiles.title: Aphids, whiteflies, or scale insects
profiles.overview: Sticky honeydew, clustered soft insects, white flying adults, or fixed bumps point to sap-feeding pests.

signals.reason: Honeydew, clusters, or fixed bumps strongly support sap feeders
Sticky residue and distorted growth fit sap feeding
Colonies can occupy tips or leaf undersides

checks: Inspect stems, growing tips, and leaf undersides with a hand lens.
Check whether fixed bumps lift away with gentle pressure.
Look for ants, which often protect honeydew-producing pests.
actions: Isolate the plant and physically remove manageable colonies.
Use a species-appropriate, label-approved soap, oil, or biological control.
Clean sticky residue and keep monitoring nearby plants for crawlers or adults.
profiles.avoid: Avoid assuming every stem bump is scale; compare with normal nodes and bark before treatment.

profiles.title: Fungus gnats and chronically damp medium
profiles.overview: Small dark flies around wet medium often signal fungus gnats and, more importantly, a root zone staying moist too long.

signals.reason: Small flies near the medium strongly support fungus gnats
Flying insects plus weak growth fit gnat pressure
Larvae thrive in consistently damp organic medium
Young roots are more vulnerable to larval feeding

checks: Confirm adults are weak fliers emerging from the medium rather than whiteflies leaving foliage.
Place a potato slice on the medium briefly to inspect for translucent larvae.
Check drainage and how long the lower pot remains wet.
actions: Let the surface dry appropriately and improve drainage without dehydrating the plant.
Use sticky cards to monitor adults and a labeled biological larvicide where permitted.
Remove decaying surface debris and correct the watering pattern that supports the population.
profiles.avoid: Avoid relying on adult traps alone; the larval habitat in the medium is the main control point.

profiles.title: Broad or russet mite pattern
profiles.overview: Severely twisted, hardened, or blistered new growth without visible webbing can come from microscopic mites.

signals.reason: Severe distortion is concentrated in tender growth
The growing tip is the center of damage
No obvious larger insect explains the injury
Some microscopic mites thrive in sheltered tender tissue

checks: Use strong magnification or a local diagnostic service; these mites can be too small for a basic hand lens.
Rule out herbicide drift, calcium stress, and heat injury.
Inspect nearby plants for a matching distortion pattern.
actions: Isolate the plant and stop moving cuttings or tools between plants.
Seek species-specific identification before choosing a miticide or biological control.
Remove severely damaged material only after containment and tool sanitation are arranged.
profiles.avoid: Avoid broad pesticide use based only on twisted leaves; several non-pest causes look similar.

profiles.title: Powdery mildew
profiles.overview: Expanding white, talc-like patches on leaf surfaces are consistent with powdery mildew.

signals.reason: White powder is the defining visible pattern
Humid, stagnant conditions support disease pressure
Patches can spread through the canopy

checks: Wipe a small area with a damp swab and inspect the margin for new powder.
Check shaded interior leaves and nearby plants.
Measure humidity swings and air movement through the canopy.
actions: Isolate the plant and bag heavily affected leaves before removal.
Improve spacing, airflow, and humidity control while keeping foliage dry.
Use a product labeled for the exact plant and disease, following harvest restrictions for edible crops.
profiles.avoid: Avoid consuming affected plant material or spraying household mixtures whose crop safety is unknown.

profiles.title: Botrytis or flower rot
profiles.overview: Gray fuzz, soft brown flower tissue, and a collapse that begins inside dense growth demand immediate containment.

signals.reason: Gray growth or soft collapse is a high-value rot signal
Flowers, buds, or fruit are affected
High humidity favors Botrytis
Cool damp periods increase risk

checks: With gloves, inspect the interior of dense flowers or fruit for brown tissue.
Check nearby sites for sudden wilted leaves emerging from the affected cluster.
Review nighttime humidity and condensation.
actions: Isolate the plant, stop fans before handling, and bag affected material at the site of removal.
Sanitize tools and restore safe spacing, airflow, and humidity control.
Discard affected consumable tissue; retain only material that is clearly healthy and permitted by local guidance.
profiles.avoid: Do not inhale, consume, compost indoors, or shake visibly moldy material through the growing area.

profiles.title: Fungal or bacterial leaf spot
profiles.overview: Discrete lesions that expand, develop halos, or spread by splash fit a leaf-spot disease more than a uniform nutrient pattern.

signals.reason: Expanding spots and halos support a leaf disease
Scattered or lower-leaf lesions fit splash spread
Long leaf-wetness periods raise disease risk
Soil splash can move inoculum onto lower leaves

checks: Mark lesion edges and see whether they expand over 48 hours.
Look for concentric rings, yellow halos, or water-soaked margins.
Inspect irrigation patterns and how long foliage stays wet.
actions: Separate affected plants and remove heavily spotted leaves with clean tools.
Water at the root zone and improve spacing so leaves dry promptly.
Use a crop-labeled disease product only after narrowing the pathogen class.
profiles.avoid: Avoid overhead watering and handling wet plants, which can spread several leaf-spot organisms.

profiles.title: Damping-off or seedling stem collapse
profiles.overview: A pinched, dark, soft stem at the medium line in a seedling is a classic damping-off emergency.

signals.reason: The plant is in the vulnerable seedling stage
Damage centers at the stem base or crown
Soft collapse at the base fits damping-off
Persistent moisture favors seedling pathogens

checks: Inspect the stem exactly at the medium line for narrowing or dark softness.
Compare affected and healthy seedlings in the same tray.
Check tray sanitation, airflow, density, and water temperature.
actions: Remove collapsed seedlings and nearby contaminated medium.
Increase gentle airflow, reduce surface saturation, and use clean trays and propagation media.
Protect unaffected seedlings with species-appropriate sanitation and a labeled biological control if available.
profiles.avoid: Avoid reusing contaminated propagation medium or trying to stand up a seedling whose stem has fully collapsed.

profiles.title: Chewing insect or slug damage
profiles.overview: Missing tissue, ragged edges, or clean holes point to a chewing pest rather than nutrition.

signals.reason: Missing leaf tissue directly supports a chewing pest
Feeding may be localized
Soil and containers can shelter night-feeding pests

checks: Inspect after dark and under leaf folds for caterpillars, beetles, slugs, or droppings.
Look for slime trails, pellets, webbed leaves, or eggs.
Confirm the holes appeared after leaves opened; torn emerging leaves can mimic chewing.
actions: Hand-remove identified pests where practical and exclude them with barriers or netting.
Use a product or biological control labeled for the identified pest and plant.
Recheck at the time of day when feeding occurs.
profiles.avoid: Avoid applying a broad insecticide before identifying whether the pest is an insect, mite, or slug.

profiles.title: Sunscald or abrupt exposure injury
profiles.overview: Bleached, papery patches on the most exposed side often follow a sudden move into direct sun.

signals.reason: Bleached, papery tissue fits sunscald
Exposure increased recently
Only exposed surfaces are damaged
Current light is intense

checks: Compare the sun-facing side with protected tissue.
Check whether damage appeared within one or two bright days after the move.
Rule out spray droplets or oil applied before strong sun.
actions: Return the plant to partial protection and acclimate it in stages.
Keep watering steady while undamaged leaves carry recovery.
Use shade cloth during peak exposure if the plant must remain outdoors.
profiles.avoid: Avoid removing every marked leaf immediately; intact green areas still support the plant.

profiles.title: Spray, herbicide, or chemical injury
profiles.overview: Sudden distortion, spotting, or bleaching after a spray or nearby treatment can be chemical injury.

signals.reason: The injury pattern can follow chemical exposure
Exposed patches are affected
A recent change may have altered exposure
No pest evidence was found

checks: Review every foliar spray, cleaner, pesticide, and nearby herbicide used in the prior week.
Look for a one-sided drift pattern or droplet-shaped spots.
Ask whether a product was applied in strong light or above its labeled temperature.
actions: Stop the suspected product and move the plant away from continued drift.
Rinse foliage promptly only when the product label and plant tolerance support it.
Document the exposure and watch undamaged new growth before adding another treatment.
profiles.avoid: Avoid combining remedies; additional sprays can make the injury harder to identify and more severe.

profiles.title: Normal leaf aging or seasonal change
profiles.overview: A small number of oldest leaves can yellow and shed as a healthy plant reallocates resources or responds to seasonal change.

signals.reason: Color change can occur during normal aging
Only the oldest leaves are involved
Mature or reproductive plants commonly retire older leaves
Roots appear healthy
Moisture appears stable

checks: Confirm that new growth remains healthy and the pattern is limited to a few oldest leaves.
Compare the rate of leaf loss with the plant's normal seasonal habit.
Recheck roots and growing tips for any sign the pattern is spreading.
actions: Remove leaves only when they release easily or are fully spent.
Keep normal care steady and track the number of affected leaves.
Escalate the diagnosis if yellowing moves rapidly upward or new growth changes.
profiles.avoid: Avoid adding fertilizer solely to keep every oldest leaf green.

profiles.title: Root-zone and environment review
profiles.overview: The current observations overlap several causes, so the safest next move is to verify root moisture, light, and climate before treating.

signals.reason: The symptom is real but shared by several conditions
Root condition has not been inspected
Root-zone pH has not been measured
Temperature needs a direct reading

checks: Record root-zone moisture, leaf-level temperature, humidity, and recent care changes.
Inspect leaf tops, undersides, stems, and the medium with bright light.
Take clear photos now so progression can be compared in 48 hours.
actions: Keep care stable while gathering the missing observations.
Correct only a clearly measured issue, starting with water, drainage, temperature, or light.
Return to the questionnaire with the new evidence for a narrower result.
profiles.avoid: Avoid applying fertilizer and pesticide together when the cause is still broad.

moisture: Stays wet for a long time
light: Very bright or close to a lamp
pestEvidence: Small dark flies near the medium
Fixed bumps on stems or leaves
rootEvidence: Roots circle the pot or fill it tightly
